Salvadoran Chemical Workers’ Walkout Disrupts Production, Hits Key Firms

A strike by chemical industry workers in El Salvador has brought significant disruption to production across the sector this week, leaving companies scrambling to meet orders and manage supply chain delays. The action, which began on Monday, stems from ongoing wage negotiations and calls for improved workplace safety, union representatives said.

TermoencogibLes SA de CV, a major producer of industrial packaging materials, confirmed that operations at its main plant in San Salvador have been “severely curtailed” since the walkout began. “We are currently operating at less than 30% capacity,” said Jorge Martínez, head of operations at TermoencogibLes SA de CV. “Our warehouse inventories are depleting quickly. If the situation continues, we will be forced to delay shipments to customers both locally and in export markets.”

The National Federation of Chemical Industry Workers (FENATIQ) estimated that over 1,200 employees at eight major firms, including TermoencogibLes, are participating in the walkout. “Our members are committed to resuming work, but only once their concerns are addressed,” said FENATIQ spokesperson Ana Castillo. She cited stagnant wages and insufficient investment in safety equipment as key grievances.

According to data from the Salvadoran Chamber of Chemical Producers, the sector generates around $180 million in annual export value. “Every day of lost production is a serious blow,” said Chamber president Ricardo López. “We urge both parties to reach a swift resolution.”

Analysts warn that a prolonged strike could impact the chemical industry’s ability to fulfill long-term contracts. “Clients in Central America and the Caribbean rely on Salvadoran chemical goods for their own supply chains,” said market analyst Gabriela Méndez. “Extended delays could push buyers toward alternative suppliers, with lasting effects on the industry’s competitiveness.”

As of Thursday afternoon, talks between union leaders and management representatives were ongoing, but no agreement had been reached. Workers remain on picket lines outside several facilities, with no immediate end to the walkout in sight.
